prize_parts.citation: For discoveries on the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the mechanism-based design of long-acting receptor agonists that made incretin therapy possible for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single prize part on B025 and keep Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. The round showed that the six of us agree on the science and differ only on the framing of one seat, which is a question about what the prize is for rather than about the evidence. The incretin arc is complete: proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic and satiety actions of GLP-1 (Holst, Drucker), the realisation that native GLP-1 is cleared within minutes by DPP-4 and the kidney, and the design of acylated, albumin-binding agonists with once-daily and then once-weekly kinetics (Knudsen), followed by independent outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal disease. The half-life problem was a biological insight that decided whether the hormone could ever be a medicine, so I read the analogue work as part of the discovery chain and not as downstream product development. The Nobel remit has always included discoveries that were shown to work in patients, and I would rather the citation say so explicitly. Maturity is settled and recognition is timely.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is not resolved by my choice. Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a discovery-stage contribution, her priority is disputed, and Habener, who is not among the credited names, is part of the same early story, so my trio can be accused of preferring the drug designer to the peptide identifier. The three of us who include Knudsen and the three who include Mojsov are making a judgment about framing that the supplied evidence cannot settle, and I cannot verify the priority claims from the credit text alone. A further risk is that an industrial contribution is read as development, which would make the citation harder to defend. A single-part prize also leaves out CAR-T and optogenetics, both of which have serious claims, but the three-person cap means any second part would force a cut to the GLP-1 trio that I think is worse than waiting.

responses.point: Keeps Mojsov in the third seat so that the prize rewards what was discovered rather than which company built the drug, and says that omitting Knudsen would look wrong only under a translational framing.
responses.response: Your distinction between discovery and company product is fair, and I take it seriously. My difficulty is that identifying the active peptide and showing the hormone is insulinotropic in humans do not by themselves explain why this field changed medicine, because native GLP-1 cannot be used therapeutically. Establishing a degradation-resistant, albumin-binding agonist is an answer to a specific biological problem, which is why I regard it as discovery. I accept that your framing is coherent if the committee wants a physiology-only prize, and I cannot rule out Mojsov's claim on priority. But a physiology-only citation would honour the hormone and not the reason it reached patients, and I think that is the weaker reading of the achievement.

responses.point: Argues the prize should reward the physiology and the active peptide, with Mojsov in the third seat, and that the discovery was made as basic science before it became a drug class.
responses.response: I agree that the biology came first and that the citation must lead with physiology, and my citation does. Where I differ is the assumption that adding the drug track turns the prize into product development. The question in round 1 was whether Knudsen's analogue design is a discovery in its own right, and I now put it more concretely: the choice to use fatty-acid acylation for albumin binding and DPP-4 resistance was a mechanistic hypothesis that could have failed, and it was tested in patients. I accept your point that I cannot verify Mojsov's priority from the supplied credit and that this limits how firmly I can reject her. If the committee shows me evidence that Mojsov, and not only Habener, was decisive for the active form, I would reconsider the seat.

responses.point: Notes that a single-achievement prize leaves out strong candidates such as CAR-T and optogenetics, and questions whether a two-part prize would be preferable given the three-person cap.
responses.response: This is the central question for round 2 and I have tried to answer it on the merits. A two-part prize under the three-person cap would mean, for example, two seats for GLP-1 and one for CAR-T, and that would drop either Knudsen or Mojsov and still leave one seat for a field with at least two defensible names. I do not think either field is served by a cut that deep, and CAR-T has the extra problem that Eshhar's priority is not among the credited names. So I would not trade away B025 attribution in order to include a second part. I keep B047 as my first alternative because its medical consequence is direct and the discovery question is cleaner than for optogenetics, but I do not think it is ready to share the ballot at this size.

responses.point: Says that if the committee recognises physiology only, his configuration is the wrong one, and that GLP-1 will win almost by default because of the opening ballots.
responses.response: I share your worry that unanimity in the opening ballots can stand in for an argument, and I do not want us to treat it that way. That is why I tested my own trio against the El-Manira trio rather than against support counts. The difference I find is that your concession on physiology only is too generous: even a physiology-first prize has to explain why GLP-1 matters, and that explanation passes through the analogue work. I would keep the citation wording explicit on both parts so that the committee can defend it either way. I also agree with you that one part is right for this ballot, because a second part would shrink the GLP-1 seats at a cost to the credit.

responses.point: Joins the Drucker, Holst and Knudsen trio but flags that Knudsen's contribution is industrial drug design rather than discovery of a mechanism, and that the priority claims on the active peptide are contested and unverified.
responses.response: Your own case against is the strongest statement of the risk I carry, and I do not think it can be waved away. I would answer it by pointing to the mechanism, since the added value of the analogue work was knowing why native GLP-1 fails and designing around that, and I would put that in the citation so it cannot be read as a product prize. I share your caution on priority, since like you I cannot verify the Mojsov and Habener claims beyond what the credited names state. Where we both land is that the exclusion is contested whichever trio we choose, and that is a reason for the committee to write the framing carefully, not a reason to choose by head count.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads B025 as physiology only or as physiology plus mechanism-based therapy design, which decides between Knudsen and Mojsov
Priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, including Mojsov and Habener, cannot be verified from the supplied material and Habener is outside the credited names
Whether Knudsen's industrial contribution will be accepted as discovery
Whether a second part such as B047 or B038 could be defended without damaging the B025 trio under the three-person cap, and whether Eshhar's absence undermines a CAR-T pair
statement.conflict_note: No new conflict. As in round 1, I worked with Paul Greengard and have about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann, a committee colleague, on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy, but none of the shortlisted candidates is credited to either of us or to me. I am a neurologist and ranked B038 second in the opening round, but I do not place it in my preferred configuration and I do not treat field familiarity as a reason for it. I do not request a recusal and none has been requested of me.
